title: Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR)
summary: Specifies CBOR, the Concise Binary Object Representation, a data format designed for very small code size, fairly small messages, and extensibility without version negotiation. This revision obsoletes RFC 7049, providing editorial fixes, clarifications, and some small additions while keeping the format compatible. It is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: CBOR is a binary format for representing structured data in compact messages. Its encoded items identify their own types, and tags let the format grow without a version negotiation step.

subtitle: A compact binary format for structured data, designed for small code and extensibility.

tldr.problem: Devices and applications need a compact way to exchange structured data without requiring a schema to decode every message.
tldr.mechanism: Each CBOR item starts with a byte that identifies its major type and additional information. Tags and simple values extend the data model while preserving a generic encoding structure.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8949 is an Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 7049 while keeping full compatibility with its interchange format. It does not create a new format version.

today: RFC 8949 is an Internet Standard (STD 94) and obsoletes RFC 7049. It keeps full compatibility with the earlier interchange format and does not define a new format version.

sections.title: Goals of CBOR
sections.content:
The Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) is a binary serialization format based on an extended version of the JSON data model. It is designed to encode common Internet data types, use compact encoder and decoder code, and allow decoding without a schema description.

CBOR aims for reasonably small messages, but keeps implementation simplicity ahead of maximum compactness. It supports JSON data types for conversion, adds byte strings, and provides extension points. The same value may have more than one valid encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: CBOR represents structured data as bytes that a decoder can understand without a separate schema. The format also aims to keep encoder and decoder code small.

sections.title: The Data CBOR Can Represent
sections.content:
The generic CBOR data model includes integers, simple values, floating-point values, byte strings, text strings, arrays, maps, and tagged items. An integer and a floating-point value remain distinct even when they have the same numeric value. The basic integer range is -2^64 through 2^64-1.

Registered simple values and tags extend the generic model. Applications define their own specific data model by choosing which items they accept and what those items mean. CBOR distinguishes an item that is well-formed from one that is valid and from one that meets an application's expectations.
sections.plainLanguage: CBOR has building blocks for numbers, text, bytes, lists, maps, and tagged values. An application chooses which of those building blocks its messages allow.

sections.title: Major Types and Initial Bytes
sections.content:
Each encoded item begins with an initial byte. Its high-order 3 bits identify the major type; its low-order 5 bits provide additional information, often the value or the length that follows. Depending on that information, an argument may be carried in the initial byte or in 1, 2, 4, or 8 following bytes.

The eight major types represent unsigned integers, negative integers, byte strings, UTF-8 text strings, arrays, maps, tags, and simple values or floating-point numbers. Arrays, maps, and strings may use indefinite length when the total size is not known at the start; a break stop code marks the end.
sections.plainLanguage: The first byte says what kind of item follows and how to read its value or length. Some arrays, maps, and strings can end with a stop code instead of a stated length.

sections.title: Tags Add Meaning to Data Items
sections.content:
A tag places a tag number before one data item to give it additional meaning. The RFC defines tags for date and time values, large integers, decimal fractions, binary fractions, and hints for converting data to other formats. For example, tag 0 marks a date-time text string, while tags 2 and 3 represent large positive and negative integers.

A decoder does not need to understand every tag. It can pass the tag number and its content to the application. The self-described CBOR tag is 55799; its encoded head is 0xd9d9f7 and can mark the beginning of CBOR data when other context is unavailable.
sections.plainLanguage: A tag adds a label that tells an application how to interpret an item, such as a date or a large integer. A decoder can pass through a tag it does not recognize.

sections.title: Preferred and Deterministic Encodings
sections.content:
Preferred serialization uses the shortest form for an argument, the shortest floating-point form that preserves the value, and a definite length when the length is known when encoding begins. CBOR does not require every encoder or decoder to use or enforce this preference.

Protocols that need one predictable byte sequence can define a deterministic encoding. The core deterministic requirements use preferred serialization, forbid indefinite-length items, and sort map keys by the bytewise lexicographic order of their deterministic encodings. A separate length-first ordering is available for compatibility with the order suggested in RFC 7049.
sections.plainLanguage: Preferred serialization uses the shortest encoding that preserves an item. A protocol can add stricter rules so different encoders produce the same bytes.

sections.title: Rules for Protocols and JSON Conversion
sections.content:
CBOR-based protocols must define how decoders handle invalid or unexpected data, including duplicate map keys. They also need to define the application's data model. This helps senders and receivers interpret the same bytes consistently.

The RFC gives non-normative advice for converting CBOR and JSON. Many types map directly, but byte strings and some tagged values need another representation. A map converts directly to a JSON object only when its keys are text strings; converting other key types to strings can create collisions.
sections.plainLanguage: A protocol must tell its decoder how to handle invalid data and repeated map keys. CBOR and JSON can be converted, but some CBOR types need a substitute or can lose information.

sections.title: Registries and Media Types
sections.content:
IANA maintains separate registries for CBOR simple values and tags. The RFC sets assignment procedures for different ranges in both registries. It also registers application/cbor as the media type for one encoded CBOR item, with the .cbor file extension.

The CoAP Content-Format identifier for CBOR is 60. Media types based on one encoded CBOR item use the structured syntax suffix +cbor.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps separate lists for CBOR's simple values and tags. The media type is application/cbor, and CoAP uses content-format identifier 60.

sections.title: Handling Untrusted Encoded Data
sections.content:
A CBOR decoder must treat all input as potentially hostile, even if it arrived over a secure channel. An item may claim an extreme size, contain deep nesting, overflow arithmetic, or trigger excessive processing. Decoders need resource limits and must stop processing when they detect malformed CBOR.

Different interpretations of duplicate keys, numbers, tags, or non-preferred encodings can also create security problems. Protocols should define one interpretation and specify their data model; applications still need to check whether input meets their own requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: A decoder must check CBOR input carefully, even when the sender seems trusted. It should limit resource use and reject malformed data before the application acts on it.

items.label: Negative integer
items.desc: The value is -1 minus the argument.

items.label: Byte string
items.desc: The argument gives the number of bytes.

items.label: Text string
items.desc: The argument gives the number of UTF-8 bytes.

items.label: Array
items.desc: The argument gives the number of data items.

items.label: Map
items.desc: The argument gives the number of key-value pairs.

items.label: Tag
items.desc: The argument is the tag number; one item follows.

items.label: Simple or float
items.desc: Carries simple values, floats, or the break code.
